headings.title: Introduction to Health Economics and Scarcity
headings.content: Health economics is a specialized branch of economics that evaluates the allocation of resources in the production and consumption of health and healthcare. In the context of nursing and healthcare delivery in Nigeria and globally, resources such as skilled personnel, hospital beds, pharmaceuticals, and government funding are inherently limited. This foundational reality is known as scarcity. Scarcity means that human wants and needs for healthcare services exceed the available resources to provide them. Because resources are finite, healthcare decision-makers, including nurse leaders and health policy planners, must constantly make choices about how to distribute care efficiently and equitably. Nurses often experience the direct impact of scarcity through heavy workloads, shortages of medical supplies, and crowded wards. Understanding health economics helps nursing students appreciate why prioritization and rationalization of care are necessary. It provides a framework for evaluating how limited budgets affect patient outcomes, healthcare access, and the overall performance of the health system. Economics does not just focus on money; it focuses on maximizing health benefits for the population using the fewest possible resources, ensuring sustainability and better quality of care.

headings.title: Opportunity Cost
headings.content: Opportunity cost is a core concept in health economics defined as the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. Because healthcare resources are scarce, choosing to spend money or time on one health intervention means sacrificing the opportunity to use those same resources for something else. For example, if a Nigerian state government decides to allocate its limited health budget to build a new specialist tertiary hospital, the opportunity cost might be the primary healthcare clinics and vaccination programs that could have been funded instead. At the clinical level, if a nurse spends an hour performing a non-clinical administrative task, the opportunity cost is the direct patient care or health education they could have provided during that time. Recognizing opportunity costs forces nurses, managers, and policymakers to think critically about resource allocation. It highlights that every healthcare decision carries a trade-off, and resources must be directed toward interventions that yield the greatest health gain for the population. Evaluating opportunity cost ensures transparency and accountability in health sector planning and clinical practice.

headings.title: Demand
headings.content: Demand in health economics refers to the quantity of healthcare goods and services that consumers are willing and able to purchase at various price levels over a given period. Unlike standard consumer goods, the demand for healthcare is often derived demand—people do not demand healthcare for its own sake, but rather for the health and well-being that it produces. Furthermore, healthcare demand has unique characteristics, such as uncertainty and asymmetry of information. Patients rarely know what treatments they need; instead, they rely heavily on healthcare providers, particularly physicians and nurses, to guide their demand. In many low- and middle-income settings, out-of-pocket payment heavily influences demand, meaning that high service costs can prevent vulnerable populations from seeking necessary care. The law of demand generally applies: as the price of a healthcare service increases, the quantity demanded tends to decrease, assuming all other factors remain constant. However, factors like disease severity, insurance coverage, and perceived quality can shift or alter how price affects a patient's decision to seek medical attention.

headings.title: Supply
headings.content: Supply in health economics represents the total quantity of healthcare goods and services that producers—such as hospitals, clinics, pharmaceutical companies, and healthcare professionals—are willing and able to offer at various price levels. The supply of healthcare is complex and heavily regulated due to the critical nature of health outcomes and patient safety. Factors influencing healthcare supply include the availability of trained personnel (like doctors, pharmacists, and nurses), technological advancements, infrastructure costs, and government health policies. For instance, an increase in the number of graduating nursing students can expand the supply of nursing care available in hospitals and community health centers. According to the law of supply, as the price or financial compensation for providing a healthcare service increases, providers are generally willing to supply more of that service. However, supply in healthcare cannot always respond quickly to market demands because training a healthcare professional or building a hospital takes substantial time and capital investment. Understanding supply dynamics helps nursing leaders anticipate staffing needs, manage resource distribution, and navigate institutional budget constraints effectively.

headings.title: Economic Price
headings.content: Economic price refers to the monetary value assigned to healthcare goods and services, reflecting both the cost of production and the market dynamics of supply and demand. In healthcare, pricing is rarely straightforward because of market failures, insurance interventions, and government subsidies. The economic price of a service encompasses direct costs—such as medications, consumables, and staff salaries—as well as indirect costs like overhead and equipment maintenance. In many healthcare systems, prices are distorted; services that are vital, such as emergency trauma care or routine immunizations, may be subsidized by the government or charity to ensure affordability, while elective procedures might carry higher profit margins. For nurses, understanding economic price is important when managing ward inventories, minimizing wastage of expensive consumables, and advocating for cost-effective patient care. When patients face high economic prices without adequate financial risk protection, they may delay seeking treatment, leading to worse health outcomes and higher overall costs when conditions become advanced. Thus, pricing strategies directly influence healthcare access, equity, and the financial viability of health institutions.

headings.title: Equilibrium
headings.content: Equilibrium in health economics occurs when the quantity of healthcare services demanded by consumers equals the quantity supplied by providers at a specific price level. At this equilibrium point, there is neither a shortage (excess demand) nor a surplus (excess supply) in the market. In a theoretical, perfectly competitive market, the price mechanism automatically adjusts to reach this balance. However, the healthcare market rarely achieves true free-market equilibrium due to unique characteristics like government intervention, insurance monopolies, and asymmetric information between patients and providers. For instance, if government price controls set healthcare service fees too low, a shortage may occur because patient demand exceeds what providers are willing to supply, resulting in long waiting lists and overworked staff. Conversely, if prices are set artificially high, a surplus of specialized services might exist while patients cannot afford them. Understanding equilibrium helps nurse managers and health economists analyze market imbalances, anticipate bottlenecks in service delivery, and design interventions to align healthcare resources with population needs.

headings.title: Externalities of Health Care
headings.content: Externalities in health care occur when the consumption or production of health services imposes costs or benefits on third parties who are not directly involved in the transaction. Externalities can be positive or negative and represent a major market failure that justifies government intervention in public health. A classic example of a positive externality is vaccination: when an individual gets vaccinated against an infectious disease like measles or polio, they not only protect themselves but also confer herd immunity, reducing the risk of infection for vulnerable members of the community, such as infants and immunocompromised patients. Because the private market often fails to account for these wider societal benefits, governments and public health agencies subsidize or mandate immunizations to ensure high uptake. Conversely, a negative externality might involve the spread of infectious diseases due to neglected treatment or environmental pollution from medical waste harming local communities. For public health nurses and community health workers, recognizing externalities is essential for designing effective immunization campaigns, health education programs, and disease containment strategies that protect the collective well-being of the population beyond individual clinical encounters.
